        <header class="article-header">
            <div class="article-category"><i class="fas fa-phone-alt"></i> Voice Phishing / Vishing</div>
            <h1>ShinyHunters Voice Phishing: How Hackers Are Bypassing MFA in Real-Time</h1>
            <p class="article-excerpt">The phone rings. "Hi, this is IT support—we need to verify your account."
                Within minutes, your MFA is compromised, your SSO credentials harvested, and attackers are inside
                your Salesforce, Slack, and email. ShinyHunters' vishing campaign has hit 100+ enterprises and shows
                no signs of stopping.</p>
            <div class="article-meta">
                <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> Campaign: Jan 2026</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-clock"></i> Published: Jan 27, 2026</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 22 min read</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-user"></i> Harish G</span>
            </div>
        </header>

        <img src="/images/articles/shinyhunters-vishing-mfa-bypass-2026.png"
            alt="ShinyHunters Voice Phishing Attack - MFA Bypass Visualization" class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <div class="critical-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> ACTIVE THREAT:</strong> As of January 2026,
            ShinyHunters is conducting an ongoing vishing campaign targeting enterprises using Okta, Google
            Workspace, and Microsoft Entra ID for SSO. Mandiant and Okta have issued warnings about custom phishing
            kits capable of intercepting MFA in real-time. At least 100 organizations have been targeted, with
            confirmed breaches at Crunchbase, SoundCloud, and Betterment.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-bullseye"></i> Executive Summary</h2>

        <p>ShinyHunters—the notorious cybercrime group behind breaches at Ticketmaster, AT&T, and Snowflake—has
            evolved their attack methodology. Their January 2026 campaign represents a significant escalation:
            <strong>voice phishing (vishing) combined with real-time MFA interception</strong>.</p>

        <p>Unlike traditional phishing that relies on emails and links, this campaign begins with a phone call.
            Attackers impersonate IT support staff, guide victims to convincing fake SSO login pages, and capture
            credentials and MFA tokens in real-time before they expire. The result? Complete account takeover
            without triggering traditional security alerts.</p>

        <div class="stat-grid">
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">100+</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Orgs Targeted</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value cyan">5+</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Confirmed Breaches</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value purple">Real-Time</span>
                <span class="stat-label">MFA Interception</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">3</span>
                <span class="stat-label">SSO Platforms Hit</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-key"></i> Key Takeaway:</strong> Traditional MFA (push notifications, SMS,
            TOTP) provides no protection against this attack. Only phishing-resistant authentication methods like
            FIDO2 security keys or passkeys can prevent these real-time interception attacks.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> Threat Actor Profile: ShinyHunters</h2>

        <div class="threat-actor-box">
            <h4><i class="fas fa-user-secret"></i> ShinyHunters (Also tracked as: UNC6040)</h4>
            <table>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Type</strong></td>
                    <td>Financially motivated cybercrime group</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Active Since</strong></td>
                    <td>2020</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Affiliation</strong></td>
                    <td>"The Com" (English-speaking cybercriminal collective)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Notable Breaches</strong></td>
                    <td>Ticketmaster (560M records), AT&T, Snowflake, Microsoft GitHub</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Primary Objective</strong></td>
                    <td>Data exfiltration and extortion</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Current Campaign</strong></td>
                    <td>SSO credential theft via vishing + real-time MFA bypass</td>
                </tr>
            </table>
        </div>

        <p>ShinyHunters has evolved significantly since their early days of exploiting misconfigured cloud storage.
            Their 2024 pivot to <strong>cloud platform extortion</strong>—particularly targeting Salesforce
            environments—demonstrated a sophisticated understanding of enterprise SaaS ecosystems.</p>

        <p>The group is linked to <strong>Scattered Spider (UNC3944)</strong>, sharing tactics, techniques, and
            potentially members. The January 2026 campaign shows clear tactical overlap with Scattered Spider's 2023
            attacks against Caesars and MGM Resorts.</p>

        <blockquote>
            "ShinyHunters has claimed credit for at least five attacks related to this campaign. After gaining
            initial access, these actors pivot into SaaS environments to exfiltrate sensitive data and then approach
            victims with extortion demands."
            <cite>— Mandiant Threat Intelligence, January 2026</cite>
        </blockquote>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-cogs"></i> Technical Analysis: The Attack Chain</h2>

        <p>This campaign is notable for its <strong>synchronization of social engineering with technical
                exploitation</strong>. Here's how it works:</p>

        <div class="attack-flow">
            <div class="flow-step">
                <div class="flow-number">1</div>
                <div class="flow-content">
                    <h4>Reconnaissance Phase</h4>
                    <p>Attackers identify target organizations and employees through LinkedIn, Hunter.io, and data
                        broker leaks. They focus on employees with access to sensitive SaaS platforms—particularly
                        those managing SSO, Salesforce, or financial systems.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="flow-step">
                <div class="flow-number">2</div>
                <div class="flow-content">
                    <h4>Initial Contact (Vishing Call)</h4>
                    <p>The victim receives a phone call from someone claiming to be IT support or help desk. Caller
                        ID is spoofed to show an internal or trusted number. The caller creates urgency: "We've
                        detected suspicious login activity on your account—I need to verify your identity."</p>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="flow-step">
                <div class="flow-number">3</div>
                <div class="flow-content">
                    <h4>Phishing Page Delivery</h4>
                    <p>The victim is directed to a fake SSO login page (Okta, Google, or Microsoft) hosted on a
                        freshly registered domain. The phishing kit is configured to proxy requests to the
                        legitimate SSO provider in real-time.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="flow-step">
                <div class="flow-number">4</div>
                <div class="flow-content">
                    <h4>Credential Harvest</h4>
                    <p>When the victim enters credentials, the phishing kit captures them and immediately submits
                        them to the real SSO provider. The legitimate provider triggers an MFA challenge.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="flow-step">
                <div class="flow-number">5</div>
                <div class="flow-content">
                    <h4>Real-Time MFA Interception</h4>
                    <p>The attacker on the phone synchronizes with the phishing kit. As the MFA prompt appears (push
                        notification, SMS, or TOTP), the attacker coaches the victim: "You should have received a
                        verification code—please read it to me" or "Go ahead and approve that login notification."
                    </p>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="flow-step">
                <div class="flow-number">6</div>
                <div class="flow-content">
                    <h4>Session Hijack</h4>
                    <p>With credentials and MFA token captured, the attacker establishes a legitimate session. They
                        may immediately enroll their own MFA device to maintain persistent access and invalidate the
                        victim's MFA.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="flow-step">
                <div class="flow-number">7</div>
                <div class="flow-content">
                    <h4>Lateral Movement & Data Exfiltration</h4>
                    <p>Using the compromised SSO account, attackers pivot to connected SaaS applications:
                        Salesforce, Slack, GitHub, Google Drive, etc. They exfiltrate valuable data, often including
                        customer PII, financial records, and intellectual property.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="flow-step">
                <div class="flow-number">8</div>
                <div class="flow-content">
                    <h4>Extortion</h4>
                    <p>Victims receive ransom demands. If payment isn't made, data is leaked on BreachForums or
                        Telegram, damaging reputation and triggering regulatory consequences.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-tools"></i> The Phishing Kit: Technical Deep Dive</h2>

        <p>The custom phishing kits used in this campaign are sophisticated adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) tools.
            Based on analysis from security researchers, here are the key technical characteristics:</p>

        <h3>Domain Patterns</h3>
        <p>Attackers register domains that closely mimic legitimate SSO providers:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><code>okta-verify-[company].com</code></li>
            <li><code>sso-[company]-login.com</code></li>
            <li><code>google-workspace-verify.com</code></li>
            <li><code>microsoft-entra-auth.com</code></li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Real-Time Proxy Architecture</h3>
        <p>Unlike static phishing pages that simply capture credentials, these kits function as <strong>reverse
                proxies</strong>:</p>
        <ol>
            <li>Victim's browser connects to the phishing domain</li>
            <li>Phishing server proxies requests to legitimate SSO provider</li>
            <li>Legitimate responses (including MFA challenges) are relayed back to victim</li>
            <li>Session cookies and tokens are captured server-side</li>
            <li>Attacker's browser receives captured session, bypassing MFA entirely</li>
        </ol>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Why Traditional MFA Fails:</strong>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Push notifications:</strong> Victim approves the prompt thinking it's legitimate</li>
                <li><strong>SMS/TOTP codes:</strong> Victim reads the code to the attacker over the phone</li>
                <li><strong>Email OTP:</strong> Captured through the same session proxy</li>
            </ul>
            The MFA challenge is real—it's happening against the legitimate provider. The victim has no indication
            they're being phished.
        </div>

        <h3>Browser Fingerprint Matching</h3>
        <p>Advanced phishing kits capture browser fingerprints (user agent, timezone, screen resolution) and replay
            them when establishing the attacker's session. This helps evade anomaly detection systems that flag
            logins from unusual devices.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-building"></i> Confirmed Victims and Targets</h2>

        <p>Silent Push researchers identified approximately <strong>100 organizations</strong> targeted in the
            January 2026 campaign. Confirmed victims include:</p>

        <div class="victim-list">
            <div class="victim-card">
                <i class="fas fa-database"></i>
                <div>
                    <span class="victim-name">Crunchbase</span>
                    <span class="victim-status">PII + Corporate Data Leaked</span>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="victim-card">
                <i class="fas fa-music"></i>
                <div>
                    <span class="victim-name">SoundCloud</span>
                    <span class="victim-status">Data Exfiltrated</span>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="victim-card">
                <i class="fas fa-piggy-bank"></i>
                <div>
                    <span class="victim-name">Betterment</span>
                    <span class="victim-status">Confirmed Breach</span>
                </div>
            </div>
            <div class="victim-card">
                <i class="fab fa-google"></i>
                <div>
                    <span class="victim-name">Google (Salesforce CRM)</span>
                    <span class="victim-status">Compromised Aug 2025</span>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>Organizations Targeted (Not Confirmed Compromised)</h3>
        <p>Silent Push identified targeting activity against these major enterprises:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Atlassian</strong> — Enterprise collaboration and development tools</li>
            <li><strong>Epic Games</strong> — Gaming and Unreal Engine</li>
            <li><strong>HubSpot</strong> — CRM and marketing platform</li>
            <li><strong>Canva</strong> — Design platform with 170M+ users</li>
            <li><strong>Iron Mountain</strong> — Data storage and protection</li>
            <li><strong>RingCentral</strong> — Cloud communications</li>
            <li><strong>ZoomInfo</strong> — B2B intelligence platform</li>
            <li><strong>Genesys</strong> — Contact center software</li>
            <li><strong>AppLovin</strong> — Mobile app monetization</li>
        </ul>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-history"></i> Timeline of Events</h2>

        <div class="timeline">
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">2020</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">ShinyHunters emerges, targeting cloud storage and developer
                    repositories</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">2024</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Pivot to cloud platform extortion, particularly Salesforce
                    environments</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">March 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Salesforce acknowledges UNC6040 campaign targeting SSO credentials via
                    social engineering</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">June 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">French authorities arrest several ShinyHunters members; copycat
                    operations continue</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">August 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">ShinyHunters compromises Google's Salesforce CRM via vishing
                    attack</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">January 2026</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Okta warns of social engineering campaign with custom phishing
                    kits</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">January 2026</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Mandiant confirms ongoing ShinyHunters vishing campaign; 100+ orgs
                    targeted</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">January 2026</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Crunchbase, SoundCloud, Betterment data leaked after extortion attempts
                    rejected</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-balance-scale"></i> Why This Attack Succeeds: The Human Factor</h2>

        <p>Security teams often focus on technical controls: email filtering, endpoint protection, network
            segmentation. This attack exploits a fundamental gap: <strong>the phone channel is largely
                undefended</strong>.</p>

        <h3>Psychological Manipulation Tactics</h3>

        <table class="comparison-table">
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Tactic</th>
                    <th>How It's Used</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Authority</td>
                    <td>Caller claims to be IT support, help desk, or security team</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Urgency</td>
                    <td>"Your account is showing suspicious activity—we need to verify now"</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Helpfulness</td>
                    <td>Attacker is polite, professional, and "helping" resolve an issue</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Consistency</td>
                    <td>Login page looks legitimate, MFA prompt is real, nothing seems wrong</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Social Proof</td>
                    <td>"Other employees had this issue too—it's a known problem"</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Why Security Training Falls Short</h3>
        <p>Most security awareness training focuses on:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Recognizing suspicious emails</li>
            <li>Checking URLs before clicking</li>
            <li>Not downloading attachments from unknown senders</li>
        </ul>

        <p>Few programs adequately cover:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Verifying the identity of inbound phone callers</li>
            <li>Understanding that MFA can be bypassed through social engineering</li>
            <li>Recognizing when a "real" SSO prompt is actually proxied through an attacker</li>
        </ul>

        <blockquote>
            "These attacks exploit user manipulation rather than platform vulnerabilities. The human is the attack
            surface."
            <cite>— Salesforce Security Advisory, March 2025</cite>
        </blockquote>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Defense Strategies</h2>

        <p>Protecting against this attack requires a multi-layered approach that addresses both technical controls
            and human factors.</p>

        <h3>Immediate Actions</h3>

        <div class="defense-grid">
            <div class="defense-card">
                <h4><i class="fas fa-key"></i> Deploy FIDO2/Passkeys</h4>
                <p>Hardware security keys (YubiKey, Google Titan) and device-bound passkeys are phishing-resistant
                    by design. They cryptographically bind authentication to the legitimate domain—fake SSO pages
                    can't trigger them.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="defense-card">
                <h4><i class="fas fa-hashtag"></i> Enable Number Matching</h4>
                <p>For push notification MFA, require users to enter a number displayed on the login screen into
                    their authenticator app. This prevents blind "approve" attacks from voice calls.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="defense-card">
                <h4><i class="fas fa-phone-slash"></i> IT Support Verification</h4>
                <p>Establish clear policies: IT will never call asking for credentials or MFA codes. Create a
                    callback process where employees hang up and call IT through official channels.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="defense-card">
                <h4><i class="fas fa-mobile-alt"></i> Monitor Device Enrollments</h4>
                <p>Alert on new MFA device registrations. If an attacker enrolls their device, rapid detection
                    allows for quick remediation before further compromise.</p>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>Long-Term Defenses</h3>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Recommended Architecture Changes:</strong>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Conditional Access Policies:</strong> Require managed devices and compliant security
                    posture for SSO access</li>
                <li><strong>Impossible Travel Detection:</strong> Alert when same account logs in from
                    geographically distant locations</li>
                <li><strong>SaaS Security Posture Management (SSPM):</strong> Monitor OAuth app authorizations and
                    API activity</li>
                <li><strong>Privileged Access Management:</strong> Require additional verification for access to
                    sensitive systems (Salesforce, financial apps)</li>
                <li><strong>Zero Trust Architecture:</strong> Never trust, always verify—even for authenticated SSO
                    sessions</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>Training Updates</h3>
        <p>Security awareness training must evolve to include:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Vishing scenarios:</strong> Simulate IT support calls and test employee responses</li>
            <li><strong>MFA education:</strong> Explain that MFA is not foolproof—codes can be captured in real-time
            </li>
            <li><strong>Verification protocols:</strong> Teach employees to verify caller identity through separate
                channels</li>
            <li><strong>Reporting culture:</strong> Encourage reporting of suspicious calls without fear of
                embarrassment</li>
        </ul>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-fingerprint"></i> Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)</h2>

        <p>While specific IOCs for the January 2026 campaign are still being published by threat intelligence
            vendors, defenders should monitor for:</p>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-search"></i> Detection Indicators:</strong>
            <ul>
                <li>Login attempts from new/unknown devices immediately after phone contact</li>
                <li>MFA device enrollment following password authentication</li>
                <li>OAuth application authorizations with broad scopes (mail.read, files.readwrite)</li>
                <li>API activity spikes in Salesforce, Slack, or Google Workspace</li>
                <li>SSO logins from VPN or hosting provider IP ranges</li>
                <li>Employees reporting IT support calls they didn't request</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>Domain Patterns to Block</h3>
        <p>Block or alert on domains matching these patterns:</p>
        <pre><code>*-okta-verify.*

-sso-login. -workspace-verify. -entra-auth. login-[yourcompany]-. verify-[yourcompany]-.

        <h2><i class="fas fa-gavel"></i> Legal and Regulatory Implications</h2>

        <p>Organizations breached through this attack vector face significant regulatory exposure:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>GDPR:</strong> Breaches involving EU citizen data must be reported within 72 hours;
                potential fines up to 4% of annual global revenue</li>
            <li><strong>CCPA/CPRA:</strong> California residents have private right of action for data breaches
                resulting from negligent security</li>
            <li><strong>SEC Disclosure:</strong> Public companies must disclose material cybersecurity incidents
                within 4 business days</li>
            <li><strong>PCI-DSS:</strong> Payment card data exposure triggers compliance audits and potential fines
            </li>
        </ul>

        <p>The use of social engineering rather than technical exploitation doesn't provide legal cover. Regulators
            increasingly expect organizations to defend against known attack patterns—and vishing has been
            documented as a threat for years.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-crystal-ball"></i> What Comes Next</h2>

        <p>This campaign signals a broader shift in attack methodology. Expect to see:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>AI-enhanced vishing:</strong> Voice cloning and deepfakes making calls even more convincing
            </li>
            <li><strong>Automation at scale:</strong> Attackers using AI to conduct simultaneous vishing campaigns
                against hundreds of targets</li>
            <li><strong>Targeting of FIDO2 enrollment:</strong> Attackers may focus on initial passkey registration
                as a new interception point</li>
            <li><strong>OAuth worm propagation:</strong> Using compromised SSO accounts to authorize malicious apps
                that spread across connected SaaS platforms</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> The Bottom Line:</strong> The combination of voice phishing
            with real-time MFA interception represents a significant evolution in social engineering attacks.
            Organizations that rely on traditional MFA without phishing-resistant factors are increasingly
            vulnerable. The time to deploy FIDO2/passkeys is now—before your organization becomes the next victim.
        </div>
